To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
barley peroxidase is a unique member of the heme peroxidase superfamily that is unable to catalyse the reaction with its primary substrate hydrogen peroxidase at pH values above 5.

the structure of barley grain peroxidise has been refined to 1.9 Å resolution and the structure at three pH values (5.5,7.5 and 8.0) has been determined to investigate its unique property of being inactive at neutral pH.

barley grain peroxidases are unable to catalyse the reaction with the substrate hydrogen peroxide at physiological pH, and this is due to a dramatic structural rearrangment of the loop region between the B and C helices.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the structure of barley grain peroxidases and their relationship to the other known peroxidase structures, particularly the active site chemistry and the structural rearrangements associated with this.
the structure of the major barley grain peroxidases (BPs) and their role as a defense mechanism against pathogenic fungi.
the structural basis of the pH-dependent activity of BP 1 and the mechanism of peroxidase action in general.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the structural rearrangement observed is a result of the inability of BP 1 to bind hydrogen peroxide, and not vice versa.

the structural differences between active and inactive peroxidases are a result of the pH-dependent protonation state of a conserved histidine residue, which in turn controls the protonation state of the distal histidine and thus the ability to form compound I.

the crystal structures of barley grain peroxidases at different pH values show that the structural basis of inactivity at pH values >5.5 is the inability of histidine 41 to adopt an orientation suitable for proton transfer from the peroxide to the heme iron.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the crystallographic data for barley grain peroxidases at different pH values have provided the first structural evidence that the pH-dependent inactivation of barley peroxidases is due to the disruption of a hydrogen bonding network between the catalytic histidine and a neighboring aspartic acid.
the crystal structure of BP 1 at pH 5, 7, and 8 has been solved, and the structural changes observed are linked to the inability of BP 1 to form compound I.

the structure of BP 1 at pH 5 is the first structure to be determined of an active plant peroxidase, that it is also the first structure to show the active site of a plant peroxidase in the ferryl state, and that the structure of inactive BP 1 at different pH values is the first example of the use of crystallography to investigate the mechanism of peroxidase catalysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the structure of BP 1 is a model for a peroxidase that is unable to form compound I.
the structure of BP 1 at pH 7 is very similar to those of horseradish and peanut peroxidases.

the crystal structure of BP 1 provides a model for understanding the structural basis of peroxidase activity and in particular for understanding the structural changes required to enable the catalytic cycle to proceed at pH values above 5.
